title: Garbage Collection
objectives: Explain generational GC and the weak generational hypothesis
Compare the main collectors (G1, ZGC, Parallel)
Recognize and fix memory leaks in a GC language

sections.markdown: Garbage Collection automatically reclaims memory held by objects that are no longer reachable, freeing developers from manual free().

## Generational GC
Most objects die young (weak generational hypothesis). The heap is split:
- **Young gen** (Eden + 2 Survivors): fast, frequent **minor GC**.
- **Old gen**: long-lived objects; slower **major/full GC**.
Objects surviving enough minor GCs are promoted to old gen.
Thinking GC means 'no memory leaks.' You still leak by keeping references alive — static collections, unremoved listeners, caches without eviction. Reachable ≠ needed.
Don't call System.gc() in production — it forces full GCs and hurts performance. Tune the collector and heap sizes, and profile with tools before guessing.

flashcards.back: Most objects die young, so collecting the young generation frequently and cheaply reclaims most garbage.
Minor GC collects the young gen (fast, frequent); major/full GC collects old gen (slower).

flashcards.front: Can a GC language leak memory?
flashcards.back: Yes — if you keep references alive (static maps, listeners, unbounded caches). Reachable but unneeded objects aren't collected.

quiz.q: Generational GC is based on the idea that…
quiz.explain: The weak generational hypothesis: most allocations become garbage quickly.

quiz.q: The default collector since Java 9 is…
quiz.explain: G1 (Garbage-First) is the default, balancing throughput and pause times.

quiz.q: A common cause of leaks in Java is…
quiz.explain: Long-lived references (static maps, listeners) keep objects reachable forever.
